newsitem.title: UK: Commonwealth suspends Sierra Leone junta.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth suspends Sierra Leone junta.

text.p: The Commonwealth suspended the Sierra Leone military junta on Friday, saying membership would only be restored when the democratically elected government was returned to power.

After two days of closed-door talks on democracy in member states, Commonwealth ministers also acknowledged growing calls by human rights groups for tougher action against Nigeria and urged Gambia to answer concerns about its political system.

Some Commonwealth countries are leery of jeopardising trade links with oil-rich Nigeria, but the ministers said a recommendation would be drawn up and presented to heads of state ahead of their October summit.
The ministers' most decisive act was in barring the military regime of Sierra Leone from attending Commonwealth meetings, effective immediately.
Civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah was toppled in a coup on May 25 and chaos has since reigned in the west African state.

The Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG), set up to monitor human rights and good governance within the Commonwealth, urged the army officers to stand down from power in Freetown and the world to deny them legitimacy.
"The group called for the immediate and unconditional reinstatement of the democratically elected government of Sierra Leone," CMAG said in a statement.

"It urged the international community to continue to deny recognition to the present illegal regime in Freetown and decided...that pending the restoration of the legitimate government, the participation of Sierra Leone in the councils of the Commonwealth would be suspended," it said.
It is extremely rare for the 53-nation Commonwealth, which largely groups former British colonies, to suspend members but aides said it was universally backed by the eight CMAG members.
"People felt it was de facto. I don't think they even quarrelled about it," said one official at the talks.
Far more contentious is how to deal with Nigeria, which was suspended from the Commonwealth two years ago after executing writer Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other minority rights activists.

Despite calls for stronger punishment -- be it Nigeria's outright expulsion from the Commonwealth or the imposition of oil sanctions -- CMAG has been hampered from acting by deep splits among its members over how best to proceed.

On Thursday, CMAG heard testimony from human rights groups, who described a deteriorating situation in Nigeria and urged decisive action. Without firm steps at a heads of state meeting in October, they said the Commonwealth would lose face.

"CMAG was urged by all to recommend ... more effective measures to be taken by the Commonwealth and the wider international community to persuade Nigeria to live up to its commitments," the ministers said in a statement.
"The information which CMAG gathered from these exchanges ... was considered to be extremely useful."
The ministers would not be drawn on what steps they favoured, saying only that nothing had been ruled out and pledging a decisive plan when they next meet in September.
"It's a very serious discussion with major implications," said Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy. "By September we will be in a position to make very firm recommendations."
On the Gambia, the ministers said they remained concerned about the lack of a fully inclusive political system.
They urged the Gambia government to lift its ban on some political parties, investigate allegations of harrassment and "demonstrate its stated commitment to human rights and the rule of law".
